title: The Odds Board
hook: It is the IPL final. Your live score page shows the score 30 seconds late, and fans in the group chat are posting spoilers before your page updates.
context: Live cricket score page for a fantasy app with up to 500,000 simultaneous viewers.
solution_brief: Replace polling with push, use SSE for one-way updates, publish once and fan out at the gateway tier, serve the hot score from cache, and make reconnects polite with backoff and jitter. Polling cost is viewers times frequency, push cost is changes. SSE for one-way streams. Pub/sub into a horizontally scaled gateway fleet. 1-second TTL cache for the hot score key. Exponential backoff with jitter on reconnect.

steps.prompt: Every browser polls /score every 30 seconds, so the page can be 30 seconds late, and fans want updates within about a second. With 500,000 viewers, what should replace the polling?
steps.context_note: The score changes only a few times a minute, but every browser asks all the time.

options.text: Poll once a second and add servers to carry the load.
Server push: send a message only when the score changes.
Poll every 5 seconds as a compromise between freshness and load.

steps.explanation: Polling once a second from 500,000 viewers is about 500,000 requests per second, nearly all answering 'nothing changed'. Push inverts the cost: work happens only when the score actually changes. A 5-second interval is still 100,000 requests per second and still leaves fans seconds behind their group chat.
steps.bottleneck_note: Polling cost scales with viewers times frequency, not with how often anything actually changes.

steps.prompt: You chose server push. The browser only receives updates (score, over, wicket) and never sends anything back on this channel. Which transport fits best?
steps.context_note: The data flows in one direction only, from the server to each viewer.

options.text: Server-Sent Events: one-way over plain HTTP with automatic reconnection.
WebSocket, which keeps a two-way connection open for any future features.
Long polling, where each update ends a request and the client opens another.

steps.explanation: Server-Sent Events are built for a one-way stream, work through ordinary HTTP infrastructure, and reconnect on their own. WebSocket is the right tool for two-way, low-latency exchange such as chat or games, but adds complexity this page does not need. Long polling reopens a request after every update and wastes work on a stream that already has a better fit.
steps.bottleneck_note: Choose the simplest transport that fits the data direction.

steps.prompt: One machine holds about 50,000 open connections, and you have 500,000 viewers. When the score changes, how does the update reach all of them?
steps.context_note: The updater now needs to reach ten times more open connections than any single machine can hold.

options.text: Publish once to pub/sub, with gateways that each hold a share of the connections and forward it.
Have the score updater open a connection to each of the 500,000 viewers and push to them directly.
Run one very large machine tuned to hold all 500,000 connections.

steps.explanation: Publishing once and letting each gateway fan the message out to its own connections keeps the producer independent of the audience size, and the gateway tier scales by adding machines. Connecting the updater to every viewer makes it the bottleneck. A single huge machine is a single point of failure and a hard ceiling.
steps.bottleneck_note: Fan-out belongs at the edge of the system, not at the source.

steps.prompt: When a wicket falls, around a million people open the page and each needs the current score straight away. That one match score is your hottest key. How do you serve it?
steps.context_note: New viewers fetch the current score when the page loads, before any push message reaches them.

options.text: From an in-memory cache and CDN with a TTL of about a second.
From the database for every viewer, since it holds the real value.
From a CDN cache of 30 seconds, matching the old polling interval.
From a cache of an hour, relying on push messages to correct it.

steps.explanation: A hot key read by millions suits a cache with a tiny TTL: staleness stays under what a viewer can notice, and the origin sees one read per window. A 30-second cache brings back the delay fans were complaining about, and viewers who load the page between pushes would see a wrong score.
steps.bottleneck_note: Hot keys should be absorbed by caches, with a TTL matched to how fresh the data must be.

steps.prompt: In the final over one gateway restarts, and its 50,000 clients all reconnect within the same second while their retry loops hammer the system. How do you stop this reconnect storm from becoming an outage?
steps.context_note: Push connections are stateful. When they drop, they all come back at once.

options.text: Reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter, and shed excess attempts.
Retry every 10 milliseconds until the connection succeeds.
Reconnect on a fixed 5-second schedule so that every client behaves predictably.
Avoid restarting gateways during a match.

steps.explanation: Backoff spaces retries out and jitter breaks the synchronisation, so 50,000 clients do not all return at the same instant. A tight loop multiplies the load on a system that is already struggling, and a fixed schedule keeps every client in lockstep. Skipping restarts cannot help when a gateway crashes on its own.
steps.bottleneck_note: Synchronised retries turn a blip into an outage. Randomise client behaviour.
